lesson_title: The Cypherpunk Ethos and Decentralized Trust

questions.question_stem: A user wants online payments that can be reversed after fraud, but also wants no institution to be able to block lawful transactions. Which lesson tradeoff does this scenario illustrate?
questions.correct_answer: Centralized intermediaries can provide verification and reversibility, but they also create censorship points and single points of failure.
incorrect_answers: Decentralized payment rails can offer fast settlement, but they still need a court-approved operator to reverse disputed transfers.
Peer-to-peer money can reduce bank fees, but it depends on a national registry that can freeze every sender account instantly.
Smart-contract payments can automate refunds, but they make one vendor responsible for approving lawful merchants and disputes.
questions.explanation: The lesson frames centralized trust as useful for verification, recordkeeping, and reversibility, while also introducing fees, control points, and high-value targets.

questions.question_stem: In the lesson's account of the cypherpunk ethos, why is privacy treated as something to build into systems rather than request from institutions?
questions.correct_answer: Because privacy depends on default technical architecture, not only on institutional promises about how data will be handled.
incorrect_answers: Because security relies on permanent centralized auditing, not only on mathematical proofs about how transactions are encrypted.
Because regulation depends on active government enforcement, not only on cryptographic designs about how software is distributed.
Because anonymity relies on strict government certification, not only on voluntary agreements about how user keys will be generated.
questions.explanation: The lesson emphasizes privacy by default through code and selective disclosure, rather than reliance on governments or corporations to grant privacy after the fact.

questions.question_stem: Why did the Crypto Wars matter to the lesson's historical argument about blockchain?
questions.correct_answer: They showed the conflict over public access to strong cryptography and helped establish code as a tool for resisting centralized control.
incorrect_answers: They proved the capability of peer-to-peer networks to distribute digital cash and helped establish mining as a method for generating currency.
They demonstrated the role of commercial networks in securing private records and helped establish banks as the main source of financial privacy.
They showed the reliance of online services on government systems and helped establish laws as the key to protecting private communication.
questions.explanation: The Crypto Wars support the lesson's theme that public cryptography and code distribution were part of the political and technical foundation for later decentralized systems.

questions.question_stem: An early digital cash service uses strong privacy-preserving cryptography but depends on one company and its banking relationships. According to the lesson, what is the main unresolved weakness?
questions.correct_answer: The service can still collapse or be shut down because its organization and partners are centralized points of failure.
incorrect_answers: The protocol can leak user identities because its algorithms and keys are weak methods of message encryption.
The network can still process transactions slowly because its hardware and bandwidth are limited resources of scale.
The database can still corrupt transfer balances because its validation and memory are unstable systems of storage.
questions.explanation: The lesson distinguishes cryptographic strength from architectural resilience: earlier systems could protect some transaction details yet remain vulnerable through central companies, servers, or banking partners.

questions.question_stem: A file-sharing network has many users exchanging files directly, but everyone must first query one central directory server. How would the lesson classify its resilience?
questions.correct_answer: It is only partially decentralized because the central directory remains a legal and technical takedown target.
incorrect_answers: It is completely censorship-resistant because the user-to-user architecture prevents a physical and financial server raid.
It is highly secure against hacking because the distributed database establishes a fast and robust network connection.
It is fully peer-to-peer in theory because the direct user traffic provides a secure and permanent encryption channel.
questions.explanation: The lesson uses hybrid P2P designs to show that a central index can preserve a single point of control even when user-to-user exchange is decentralized.

questions.question_stem: Which description best captures the lesson's claim about Bitcoin's originality?
questions.correct_answer: Bitcoin combined existing cryptography, cypherpunk goals, peer-to-peer networking, past digital-cash lessons, and proof-of-work to solve decentralized agreement over transaction history.
incorrect_answers: Bitcoin introduced novel hashing functions, server infrastructure, global regulatory frameworks, corporate governance, and digital signatures to enable absolute financial anonymity for online shoppers.
Bitcoin replaced central banks, courts, wire networks, currency issuers, and payment processors to eliminate all international fees for online shoppers and merchants worldwide.
Bitcoin bypassed traditional database software, public key protocols, decentralized file networks, early cryptographic tools, and central servers to establish instant settlement for credit accounts.
questions.explanation: The lesson presents Bitcoin as a combination of prior technical and ideological ingredients, with proof-of-work enabling leaderless consensus against double-spending.

questions.question_stem: In the lesson, what specific problem does proof-of-work help solve for a decentralized digital money network?
questions.correct_answer: It helps a leaderless network converge on one transaction history, making double-spending difficult without a trusted intermediary.
incorrect_answers: It allows a centralized exchange to verify each account balance, making anonymous transactions impossible without a licensed administrator.
It forces a distributed database to encrypt all messages locally, making observation impossible without a private key.
It requires a software provider to update every system parameter, making unauthorized distribution difficult without a legal copyright license.
questions.explanation: Proof-of-work is presented as the mechanism that lets strangers coordinate on a shared history without a central leader, addressing double-spending in an open P2P environment.

questions.question_stem: A student says, "Bitcoin has no names on-chain, so it is completely anonymous." What is the best correction based on the lesson?
questions.correct_answer: Bitcoin is pseudonymous: activity is tied to identifiers on a public ledger, and those identifiers can sometimes be linked to real people.
incorrect_answers: Bitcoin is encrypted: information is hidden from participants on a closed database, and those databases can easily be decrypted by private keys.
Bitcoin is anonymous: metadata is removed from transactions on a global network, and those transactions can never be matched to IP addresses.
Bitcoin is private: identities are verified by banks on a secure interface, and those banks protect every personal detail online.
questions.explanation: The lesson separates pseudonymity from anonymity. Public blockchain records can support tracing even when real-world names are not directly written into transactions.

questions.question_stem: A user buys cryptocurrency through an exchange, leaves funds in an exchange account, and relies on the exchange for recovery support. What does this show about the lesson's "promise versus reality" theme?
questions.correct_answer: Even if the base protocol reduces intermediaries, the surrounding ecosystem can reintroduce centralized trust relationships.
incorrect_answers: Even if the public database guarantees complete privacy, the underlying network can expose sensitive transaction metadata.
Even if the consensus mechanism prevents fraud, software developers can change basic network rules through forced upgrades.
Even if the mining process secures agreement, regulators can impose traditional banking procedures on every node.
questions.explanation: The lesson notes that blockchains did not eliminate all intermediaries; exchanges and wallet providers can become new points of custody, control, and reliance.

questions.question_stem: Why does the lesson say decentralized systems require a different threat model from traditional online banking systems?
questions.correct_answer: Attackers may target consensus rules, majority control, and incentives rather than only a central database or server perimeter.
incorrect_answers: Regulators may enforce licensing laws, corporate standards, and taxation rather than only a national currency or federal reserve.
Developers may update software codes, protocol designs, and databases rather than only a single system application or user interface.
Customers may demand faster transfers, lower fees, and pseudonymity rather than only a secure wallet deposit service.
questions.explanation: Decentralization can reduce some single-server risks, but it creates protocol-level and economic attack surfaces such as consensus manipulation.

questions.question_stem: In Hughes's argument, what distinguishes privacy from secrecy?
questions.correct_answer: Privacy is selective disclosure: revealing identity or information when appropriate, rather than hiding everything from everyone.
incorrect_answers: Secrecy is permanent anonymity: protecting messages or software from public exposure, rather than sharing everything with governments.
Security is local responsibility: enforcing compliance or rules under strict authorities, rather than relying entirely on cryptography.
Anonymity is complete isolation: hiding transaction metadata under concealment rather than revealing identity to partners.
questions.explanation: The reading defines privacy as control over what is revealed and when, which allows voluntary identity disclosure instead of total concealment.

questions.question_stem: Which online transaction design best follows the reading's data-minimization principle?
questions.correct_answer: The system reveals only the information needed to complete the transaction, while avoiding unnecessary identity and relationship data exposure.
incorrect_answers: The provider collects all the credentials required to authorize the customer, while promising absolute confidentiality and government audit compliance.
The software publishes all the transaction metadata to secure the consensus, while encrypting basic messaging content and private routing information.
The protocol requires identity verification to establish a trusted relationship, while maintaining detailed transfer histories and audit logs.
questions.explanation: Hughes argues that electronic transactions should disclose only what the transaction requires because aggregation of extra information undermines privacy.
questions.lesson_block: Reading: Transaction Design And Data Minimization

questions.question_stem: According to Hughes, why can digital signatures fit within a privacy-preserving system rather than contradict it?
questions.correct_answer: They allow assured identity disclosure when a user chooses to authenticate, while default transactions can still minimize identity exposure.
incorrect_answers: They enforce constant government verification when a system registers to operate, while private transactions can still bypass regulatory oversight.
They ensure permanent message encryption when a sender intends to communicate, while public directories can still facilitate message transmission.
They replace financial anonymity when a bank demands verification, while decentralized systems can still remove intermediaries.
questions.explanation: The reading pairs anonymous transaction systems with digital signatures: privacy can include chosen authentication rather than constant identity exposure.
